Local Tangent Space Alignment

Source: vignettes/articles/LTSA.Rmd
LTSA.Rmd

Here’s one recipe for building an embedding of a dataset in a lower-dimensional space:

  • Find a neighborhood (a patch) around each observation.
  • Create an approximate local chart: a map from each neighborhood to coordinates in the lower-dimensional space.
  • Transform each chart’s coordinates into a global coordinate system. Because a given point can appear in several charts, the coordinates for the same point in different charts need to agree as much as possible.

A collection of charts that cover a manifold is called an atlas and finding the transformations that relate the charts is the global alignment problem. Technically, because we are sampling points from the actual manifold, the charts and the atlas are only approximate, but this should give a sense of the vocabulary used in the literature.

Local Tangent Space Alignment (LTSA), by Zhang and Zha, goes about this by finding the nearest neighbors of each observation and using PCA to create the charts. It then chooses global coordinates that minimize the disagreement with those charts. With suitable constraints to keep the embedding from collapsing, this becomes an eigenvalue problem. Let’s see how that happens, then connect the calculation to the choices available in flotsam.

Local PCA

Let’s start with a data matrix XX containing NN observations in rows and pp features in columns. For each observation, find a neighborhood of kk observations, where kk is n_neighbors. By default, this count includes the observation itself.

Center the columns of each k×pk \times p neighborhood matrix and compute its singular value decomposition. Keep the dd left singular vectors associated with the largest singular values, where dd is ndim, and put them in a k×dk \times d matrix UiU_i for neighborhood ii. These describe how the observations are arranged along the local tangent directions.

For now, assume the neighborhood has at least dd nonzero singular values. The columns of UiU_i are then centered and orthonormal:

𝟏k𝖳Ui=0,Ui𝖳Ui=Id, \mathbf{1}_k^{\mathsf T}U_i = 0, \qquad U_i^{\mathsf T}U_i = I_d,

where 𝟏k\mathbf{1}_k is a column of kk ones and IdI_d is the d×dd \times d identity matrix. Ordinary PCA scores would also multiply these columns by their singular values, but for alignment we can work with UiU_i alone (we’ll see why when we write down the fit). If you are following along with the paper, it puts observations in columns, so our left singular vectors correspond to its right singular vectors.

So far we have done a lot of small PCAs. We now need to find global coordinates that agree as well as possible with all those local descriptions. Each observation gets one global position, however many charts it appears in. We can think of alignment as choosing one transformation per neighborhood, with those shared observations tying the transformations together.

What are we trying to align?

Each local PCA gives us coordinates in a tangent plane. We want to relate those coordinates to one global coordinate system.

The paper motivates this using a first-order Taylor approximation: over a small enough neighborhood, the smooth relationship between tangent-plane coordinates and the desired global coordinates can be approximated by a linear transformation plus a translation. This is an affine transformation. It allows stretching and shearing as well as rotations, reflections and translations, so LTSA can fit local coordinate changes that do not preserve distances.

To add some notation to the discussion, put the proposed global coordinates in an N×dN \times d matrix YY, with one observation per row. Let YiY_i contain the kk rows belonging to neighborhood ii, in the same order as the rows of UiU_i. These are coordinates we are trying to find.

Within this neighborhood, we want to be able to write

Yi≈𝟏kci𝖳+UiAi, Y_i \approx \mathbf{1}_k c_i^{\mathsf T} + U_i A_i,

where cic_i is a vector of dd offsets and AiA_i is a d×dd \times d matrix. Multiplying by AiA_i does the linear transformation, and 𝟏kci𝖳\mathbf{1}_k c_i^{\mathsf T} adds the same translation to every observation in the neighborhood. Each neighborhood gets its own cic_i and AiA_i.

Because the transformation AiA_i allows for stretching and shearing, we can use UiU_i directly, rather than multiplying its columns by their singular values as we would for PCA scores. That multiplication just rescales the local coordinate axes, but that scaling is absorbed into AiA_i.

Measuring the misfit

We now have NN affine transformations to fit, one per neighborhood, with shared observations tying the fits together. For a proposed global embedding YY, each transformation must try to reproduce the corresponding rows YiY_i.

For each neighborhood, we want to find the affine transformation that brings its local chart as close to YiY_i as possible in the least-squares sense. The differences between the proposed coordinates and the transformed chart form the residual matrix RiR_i,

Ri=Yi−𝟏kci𝖳−UiAi. R_i = Y_i-\mathbf{1}_k c_i^{\mathsf T}-U_iA_i.

Like YiY_i and UiU_i, RiR_i is a k×dk \times d matrix: one row per observation and one column per embedding axis. Each entry is a proposed coordinate minus the corresponding coordinate predicted by the affine fit. To get the best transformation, we minimize its squared Frobenius norm, ∥Ri∥F2\|R_i\|_F^2 (the sum of the squared errors across all observations and embedding axes).

Working with UiU_i makes the best fit easy to compute. Because the columns of UiU_i are centered, the best translation is given by the column means of YiY_i. Because the columns of UiU_i are orthonormal, the best linear fit is the projection of each column of YiY_i onto the space spanned by those columns. The fitted translation and coefficient matrix are:

ci=1kYi𝖳𝟏k,Ai=Ui𝖳Yi. c_i = \frac{1}{k}Y_i^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{1}_k, \qquad A_i = U_i^{\mathsf T}Y_i.

Substituting these into the residual gives us:

Ri=Yi−𝟏k𝟏k𝖳kYi−UiUi𝖳Yi=(Ik−𝟏k𝟏k𝖳k−UiUi𝖳)Yi=WiYi \begin{aligned} R_i &= Y_i - \frac{\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^{\mathsf T}}{k}Y_i - U_iU_i^{\mathsf T}Y_i \\ &= \left(I_k-\frac{\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^{\mathsf T}}{k} -U_iU_i^{\mathsf T}\right)Y_i \\ &= W_i Y_i \end{aligned}

where the LTSA residual projector, WiW_i, is defined as:

Wi=Ik−𝟏k𝟏k𝖳k−UiUi𝖳. W_i = I_k-\frac{\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^{\mathsf T}}{k}-U_iU_i^{\mathsf T}.

WiW_i is a k×kk \times k matrix that depends only on the local chart UiU_i. Multiplying it by the neighborhood coordinates YiY_i gives the residual matrix RiR_i after the best affine fit. There are two subtractions here. The term 𝟏k𝟏k𝖳Yi/k\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^{\mathsf T}Y_i/k repeats the neighborhood’s mean position in every row. Subtracting it centers the neighborhood: we move its centroid to the origin without changing the positions of the points relative to one another. The term UiUi𝖳YiU_iU_i^{\mathsf T}Y_i then subtracts the part explained by the local chart’s linear fit. What remains is the coordinate error that the best affine transformation cannot explain.

This also explains why translating the whole neighborhood does not change its fitting error. Adding the same offset to every point shifts the mean by that offset too, so centering cancels it.

If the transformed chart can reproduce YiY_i exactly, WiYiW_iY_i is a matrix of zeros. Otherwise, ∥WiYi∥F2\|W_iY_i\|_F^2 gives us a single number: the smallest sum of squared errors that any affine fit to this chart can achieve. WiW_i therefore lets us score how well the proposed embedding agrees with the local chart.

Putting the neighborhoods together

We can now score a proposed global embedding YY by adding the best-fit errors from all the neighborhoods:

E(Y)=∑i∥WiYi∥F2. E(Y)=\sum_i\|W_i Y_i\|_F^2.

To combine these errors, we can use two properties of WiW_i. First, the residual RiR_i has zero column means and no components along the columns of UiU_i. This is by construction: it is what remains after subtracting the fitted translation and the projection onto the columns of UiU_i. This makes WiW_iidempotent: applying WiW_i again to the resulting residual leaves it unchanged, i.e. Wi(WiYi)=WiYiW_i \left(W_i Y_i\right) = W_i Y_i. Therefore Wi2=WiW_i^2 = W_i.

Second, each term in the definition of WiW_i is symmetric, so Wi𝖳=WiW_i^{\mathsf T} = W_i.

For any real matrix MM the Frobenius norm is related to the trace (sum of the diagonal elements) by ∥M∥F2=tr⁡(M𝖳M)\|M\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(M^{\mathsf T}M). For our residual matrix Ri,R_i, each diagonal entry of Ri𝖳RiR_i^{\mathsf T}R_i is the sum of squared residuals for one embedding axis. With this relationship and the idempotence and symmetry of WiW_i, we have:

∥WiYi∥F2=tr⁡(Yi𝖳Wi𝖳WiYi)=tr⁡(Yi𝖳WiYi). \|W_i Y_i\|_F^2 =\operatorname{tr}(Y_i^{\mathsf T}W_i^{\mathsf T}W_i Y_i) =\operatorname{tr}(Y_i^{\mathsf T}W_i Y_i).

So that’s the cost function for a single neighborhood, simplified. The total cost of the global alignment is the sum of the costs for all neighborhoods. This can be written in terms of the full embedding matrix YY by assembling the local costs into a global alignment matrix. Create an initially zero N×NN \times N matrix BB. Add the entries of each WiW_i to the rows and columns belonging to that neighborhood’s observations:

E(Y)=∑itr⁡(Yi𝖳WiYi)=tr⁡(Y𝖳BY). E(Y)=\sum_i\operatorname{tr}(Y_i^{\mathsf T}W_i Y_i) =\operatorname{tr}(Y^{\mathsf T}BY).

That is what BB measures: the total squared error left after giving every neighborhood its best local affine fit to the same global embedding. It is symmetric because each WiW_i contributes to it symmetrically, and positive semidefinite since this error is a sum of squares, so can never be negative.

Avoiding the trivial solution

There is a trivial solution to the global alignment problem: give every observation the same global position. This is the same as giving every neighborhood the same translation and Ai=0A_i=0. The fitting error is zero, but an embedding that smushes every observation on top of each other is not useful.

Let’s first prevent all the coordinates from shrinking to zero by requiring each column of YY to have unit length. On top of that, if you embed into more than one dimension, you need to make sure that axes don’t repeatedly find the same solution. So we also require the columns to be orthogonal. Together, you can express those conditions as:

Y𝖳Y=Id. Y^{\mathsf T}Y=I_d.

These conditions rule out the all-zero embedding, but a unit-length column can still have the same value in every row. We’ll deal with that remaining problem when we choose the coordinates.

Why eigenvectors?

We now have something useful to minimize, but how do we minimize it? Start with one embedding axis, represented by a column vector yy. Its alignment cost is y𝖳Byy^{\mathsf T}By, and its unit-length constraint is y𝖳y=1y^{\mathsf T}y=1. For now, let’s minimize the cost subject to just that constraint. As is typical with constrained optimization, we’ll introduce a Lagrange multiplier, λ\lambda:

ℒ(y,λ)=y𝖳By−λ(y𝖳y−1). \mathcal{L}(y,\lambda) =y^{\mathsf T}By-\lambda(y^{\mathsf T}y-1).

For a general real square matrix MM, ∇y(y𝖳My)=(M+M𝖳)y\nabla_y\left(y^{\mathsf T}My\right) = \left(M+M^{\mathsf T}\right)y, so if MM is symmetric, ∇y(y𝖳My)=2My\nabla_y\left(y^{\mathsf T}My\right) = 2My.

At a constrained minimum, the derivatives with respect to yy and λ\lambda must vanish. Because BB is symmetric, differentiating with respect to yy gives

∇yℒ=2By−2λy=0. \nabla_y\mathcal{L}=2By-2\lambda y=0.

Rearranging gives the equation for an eigenvector:

By=λy. By=\lambda y.

So the coordinate vector for a single axis is a unit-length eigenvector of BB, with λ\lambda as the eigenvalue. At any such eigenvector, the alignment cost is the eigenvalue:

y𝖳By=y𝖳(λy)=λy𝖳y=λ. y^{\mathsf T}By =y^{\mathsf T}(\lambda y) =\lambda y^{\mathsf T}y =\lambda.

So minimizing the cost subject to unit length means selecting an eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue. Its entries supply the coordinates for that axis. But there is a catch.

If every observation has the same coordinate, subtracting the neighborhood mean leaves zeros, so each local fit has zero residual. In symbols, Wi𝟏k=0W_i\mathbf{1}_k=0, and assembling the local projectors gives B𝟏N=0B\mathbf{1}_N=0. The constant vector is therefore an eigenvector with eigenvalue zero. Scaling it to 𝟏N/N\mathbf{1}_N/\sqrt{N} gives it unit length, so it satisfies our constraint and achieves the smallest possible cost. Yet every observation still has the same coordinate. This is the remaining collapsed solution we need to exclude.

When the constant direction is the only zero mode, the recipe is simple: order the eigenpairs from smallest eigenvalue upwards, discard the first eigenvector, and take the next one for a 1-dimensional embedding.

Because BB is symmetric, we can choose its eigenvectors to be orthonormal. Each remaining eigenvector yy is then orthogonal to the constant vector, which means

𝟏N𝖳y=0. \mathbf{1}_N^{\mathsf T}y=0.

The left-hand side is just the sum of the coordinates, so their mean is zero. The remaining eigenvectors are already centered: discarding the constant eigenvector takes care of that for us.

The argument above extends to several embedding axes because the total cost is the sum of their individual costs. The orthogonality constraint prevents us from choosing the same direction repeatedly. So if you want dd coordinates, you exclude the constant direction and take the dd orthonormal eigenvectors with the lowest eigenvalues in the remaining space. Their eigenvalues add up to the total alignment cost.

We can now write the full optimization problem:

minYtr⁡(Y𝖳BY)subject toY𝖳Y=Id,Y𝖳𝟏N=0. \min_Y \operatorname{tr}(Y^{\mathsf T}BY) \quad\text{subject to}\quad Y^{\mathsf T}Y=I_d,\qquad Y^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{1}_N=0.

Here, the centering constraint Y𝖳𝟏N=0Y^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{1}_N=0 records the property that our selected eigenvectors already have.

Other zero modes

The constant direction isn’t necessarily the only one with a zero eigenvalue. Maybe you have sampled so beautifully from a pristinely flat manifold that a real solution with a nonconstant coordinate vector also has zero alignment error. Additionally, disconnected groups of neighborhoods, or other degeneracies, can give us additional zero modes.

With several zero modes, the solver can return an orthonormal basis for that zero eigenspace without making the constant vector a separate column. Several of those vectors can contain a constant component, so discarding just one of them need not leave centered coordinates. The eigenvectors with nonzero eigenvalues are still orthogonal to the constant vector and already centered.

To handle this, flotsam projects the constant direction out of the candidate vectors and then finds the lowest-cost orthonormal directions within their remaining span. This enforces centering while keeping any useful zero-cost directions.

The recipe

With the fitting problem established, the calculation is fairly compact:

  1. Find a neighborhood for each observation.
  2. Center each neighborhood and retain its first dd left singular vectors in UiU_i.
  3. Form Wi=Ik−𝟏k𝟏k𝖳/k−UiUi𝖳W_i=I_k-\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^{\mathsf T}/k-U_iU_i^{\mathsf T}.
  4. Add each WiW_i into the corresponding rows and columns of BB.
  5. Exclude the constant direction and find dd orthonormal eigenvectors of BB with the lowest eigenvalues in the remaining space.
  6. Put those vectors into the columns of YY; its rows are the embedded observations.

Some practicalities

The rest of the article connects ordinary LTSA to the choices available in ltsa(): building neighborhoods, choosing dimensions and solving the eigenproblem.

Choosing the neighbors

The local approximation depends on which observations go into each neighborhood. nn_method = "nnd" is the default and uses approximate nearest-neighbor descent, making it useful for larger datasets. For smaller examples, nn_method = "exact" compares all observations exhaustively and gives us exact, deterministic neighbors.

You can also reuse a neighbor graph across fits by passing it as nn_method. This can be a 1-based neighbor index matrix, an object containing an idx matrix, or a sparse adjacency matrix from the Matrix package. A sparse graph must have the same number of off-diagonal neighbors in every row; the edge weights are ignored. See the reference for the input formats.

How many neighbors? We need at least ndim + 2: one direction is taken up by the constant vector, ndim more by the tangent space, and we need something left over for the residual. That is only a minimum. Small neighborhoods that don’t overlap enough can leave disconnected groups or global directions that are hard to distinguish. Increasing n_neighbors may help, but it also asks a flat local approximation to cover a larger piece of the data. It changes the model, so more neighbors aren’t automatically better.

We also assumed that every centered neighborhood had at least dd nonzero singular values. When a neighborhood has numerical rank r<dr<d, flotsam uses the rr supported directions and issues a warning. The same residual-projector formula applies with a k×rk \times r matrix UiU_i and an r×dr \times d coefficient matrix AiA_i. With output = "result", assembly$rank_deficient_count and assembly$min_local_rank tell you how often this happened and the smallest local rank. These are reasons to reconsider the tangent dimension or neighborhoods before interpreting the embedding.

Are you your own neighbor?

By default, yes: include_self = TRUE includes each observation in its own neighborhood. With include_self = FALSE, the observation is left out, but n_neighbors still counts the observations actually used in the local PCA. A precomputed self-first index matrix therefore needs n_neighbors + 1 columns: the first column contains the observation itself and is removed before assembly. With include_self = TRUE, a precomputed matrix instead has n_neighbors columns and must include the observation’s own index somewhere in each row.

This apparently small bookkeeping choice also has a mathematical connection: work by Zhang and co-workers relates it to Hessian Locally Linear Embedding. For our purposes, the thing to remember is that it changes the neighborhoods used to build BB.

How many dimensions?

There are three parameters controlling the number of dimensions at different stages of the calculation. I don’t want to overcomplicate things, so if you just want a scatterplot or have already chosen the number of output dimensions, start with ndim. For a 2D scatterplot, the default is already ndim = 2. The other two parameters are for more advanced uses where you want to inspect extra global coordinates or check the numerical stability of the result.

  • ndim: the requested local tangent dimension and the number of coordinates returned as embedding. This is dd in the discussion above. Changing ndim changes the local tangent spaces, the WiW_i matrices, and hence BB.
  • spectral_dim: the number of global coordinates retained, so you can inspect extra coordinates and diagnostics to see whether the displayed embedding cuts through a group of directions with similar eigenvalues. It defaults to ndim, but can be larger if you use output = "result". The larger set is returned as spectral_embedding, and its first ndim columns form embedding.
  • eig_k: the number of candidate vectors supplied to postprocessing, before removing the constant direction and refining and selecting the coordinates. This is effectively a numerical solver parameter: a larger value gives the calculation more candidates to work with, at greater computational cost. It doesn’t change BB or the number of output coordinates.

Iterative solvers request eig_k candidates. The dense solver computes the full eigensystem and passes its lowest eig_k eigenvectors to postprocessing.

Increasing spectral_dim keeps more global coordinates from the same BB. It can help us assess the global view, but it doesn’t establish whether ndim was sufficient for the local projections. Changing that local dimension means changing ndim and rebuilding BB.

spectral_dim must be at least ndim. When it is larger, eig_k must be at least spectral_dim + 2: one extra place for the constant direction and another for the mode just beyond the retained coordinates, so we can check the eigenvalue gap there. When spectral_dim = ndim, the minimum is eig_k = ndim + 1. In either case, eig_k must be less than the number of observations. Most of the time you can leave it at its default.

For example, with ndim = 2, spectral_dim = 4, and eig_k = 8, we build BB using two-dimensional local projections, use eight candidate vectors for postprocessing, and retain four nonconstant global coordinates. The first two go into embedding, and all four go into spectral_embedding. The spectral blocks article gives examples of inspecting these extra coordinates.

Getting more than a picture

By default, ltsa() returns a coordinate matrix with NN rows and ndim columns. To see how the calculation went, use output = "result". For example, given a data matrix X, this keeps the default two-dimensional tangent model and embedding while retaining four global coordinates:

fit <- flotsam::ltsa(X, output = "result", spectral_dim = 4)

fit$embedding
fit$spectral_embedding
fit$eigen$status
fit$eigen$spectral$status
fit$eigen$messages
fit$assembly$component_count
fit$assembly$rank_deficient_count

The displayed embedding is exactly the first ndim columns of spectral_embedding. When we keep extra coordinates like this, eigen describes the displayed embedding and eigen$spectral describes the larger set. That lets us check whether a two-dimensional view is well determined even when we have retained a larger, more stable group of directions.

If you want to work with the matrix yourself, output = "B" stops before eigenanalysis and returns BB. Alternatively, use include_B = TRUE with output = "result" to include BB alongside the embedding and diagnostics.

Computing the eigenvectors

Once we have chosen the neighborhoods and tangent dimension, we have specified the alignment problem. eig_method chooses how to solve its eigenproblem.

The default, eig_method = "auto", uses dense base::eigen() for small datasets or when we ask for a large fraction of the available eigenvectors. Otherwise it uses RSpectra. Explicit requests for "rspectra", "irlba", "svdr", or dense "eig" always use the named method. If you want to check what happened, a detailed result records the requested method in eigen$method and the backend that actually ran in eigen$backend$name.

There are also controls for convergence, the thresholds used by "auto", and diagnostic tolerances. If you need to investigate those, Diagnosing suspicious LTSA results connects the status, message, eigenvalue gap, component, and rank diagnostics to things you can try.

Using more cores

n_threads controls neighbor search, while n_assembly_threads controls construction of BB. Both default to serial execution. More threads change how the work is carried out, with one qualification: multithreaded approximate neighbor search need not produce exactly the same graph on each run, so the embedding can change too. If you are comparing settings, reusing a precomputed graph removes that source of variation.

The threading guidance also covers what happens when BLAS wants to use several cores at the same time as the assembly code. More threads aren’t automatically better here either.
